title: Home in ordinary clothes
hook: back at Kartarpur, Nanak lays down the pilgrim's robe and lives as a householder (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, karah prashad, and your line, worlds beyond worlds. Did you look up last night? Today the traveler comes home. Day seven hundred four.

The suitcase goes down in the hall. The shoes come off. The clothes you traveled in, the ones that smell of trains and other people's cities, go into the wash, and you pull on the soft old things you only wear at home. There's a particular relief in that moment: the trip is over, and ordinary life can start again. Bhai Gurdas gives Guru Nanak that moment too, after the mountain, Mecca and Baghdad. Today: udasi.
screen: `THE SUITCASE IN THE HALL.` → `TRAVEL CLOTHES OFF.` → `ORDINARY LIFE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas says: then Baba came to Kartarpur, and took off the whole garb of the udasi, the wandering renunciant. He put on the clothes of a householder, worldly clothes, and sat on a manji, a simple cot, and taught from there. Year one told you about the farmer at Kartarpur, working the land by the river. Today, look closely at the clothes. On the road, Nanak wore the wanderer's garb. At home, he takes that off. Nothing about him now says holy man to a passerby. He looks like anyone in the village. And Bhai Gurdas doesn't treat this as a step down. He tells it as the point. The holiness didn't live in the robe, so taking the robe off costs nothing. Then he tells what daily life at Kartarpur sounded like, and if you've just finished year two, listen to this. Bhai Gurdas says the Guru's word was spoken there, and light spread and darkness went. And Sodar and Aarti, the evening hymns, were sung, and the Japji was recited at amritvela, the early hours before dawn. That's the shape of the day you learned all last year: the Japji before sunrise, the evening prayers at dusk. In Bhai Gurdas's telling, it's already there at Kartarpur, kept by a man in ordinary clothes, in an ordinary village, between the farming and the meals. Holiness came home, and it looked like a routine.
screen: `THE UDASI'S ROBE COMES OFF.` · `A HOUSEHOLDER, ON A SIMPLE COT.` · `THE HOLINESS WASN'T IN THE ROBE.` · `JAPJI AT DAWN, SODAR AT EVENING.` · then, large: `HOLY IN ORDINARY CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one ordinary task with devotion. Pick something small that's right in front of you. Wash one cup. Fold one shirt. Wipe one counter. Water one plant. Do it slowly, with your full attention, as if it were the most important thing in the house, because for the next two minutes, it is. Notice your hands, the water, the cloth. No special clothes, no special place. If you pray, you can let Waheguru ride along with each movement. The bell holds the time.
Udasi, the wandering renunciant's garb Nanak set aside at Kartarpur, taking up a householder's clothes and keeping the daily prayers there.
Your line: holy in ordinary clothes. Today, choose one plain chore you usually rush, and do it once as if it mattered. Day seven hundred four.

howItsDone: Sikhs live as householders rather than renunciants, working, raising families and keeping the daily banis at home, and they point to Guru Nanak's life at Kartarpur as the pattern.

fork.setup: you're coming home after years on the road as a famous holy traveler. what do you wear now?
options: the traveler's robe, so people know who you are.
ordinary clothes, like everyone in the village.
something grander, for a teacher with followers.
fork.reveal: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak took off the whole garb of the udasi and put on worldly clothes. the holiness wasn't in the robe.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a wandering renunciant. Bhai Gurdas says Nanak took off the udasi's garb at Kartarpur.

trapdoor: what you thought: the traveler settles down and the story slows.
what it means: setting aside the robe is the point. holiness came home and looked like an ordinary day.
what a scholar hears: Bhai Gurdas names the Japji at amritvela, and Sodar and Aarti sung, in Kartarpur itself, an early witness to a daily pattern.
recall: the Guru's word for the day

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 38 (Kartarpur: the udasi's garb set aside; Sodar, Aarti and the Japji)

notes: Var 1 pauri 38 paraphrased from memory: phir baba aaiaa Kartarpur, bhekh udaasee sagal utaaraa; pahir sansaaree kapre manjee baith keeaa avtaaraa; baanee mukhahu uchaareeai hoi rushnaaee mitai andhaaraa; sodar aartee gaaveeai amrit vele jaap uchaaraa. Confirm the pauri number and paraphrase.
'Manji' glossed as a simple cot from which he taught; confirm.
'Aarti' here refers to the evening hymns (as in Kirtan Sohila), not a lamp ritual; the script does not explain this. A Keeper may want a clarifying phrase.
Year 1 day 41 covered farming at Kartarpur; this day keeps to the clothes and the daily banis to avoid repeating it.
'An early witness to a daily pattern' in the trapdoor is phrased softly; confirm.
Editor: cut unsourced 'people could see from a distance what he was'; glossed Sodar and Aarti as evening hymns so 'Aarti' is not heard as a lamp ritual.

Audit (day 704): the pauri times only the Japji (amrit vele); the script had Bhai Gurdas place Sodar and Aarti 'at dusk', so the timing is no longer attributed to him (teach, screen head, trapdoor). Cut 'this first telling', an unsourced first-ever claim.
